entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6252"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 69</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.69.1-Ps.69.36">Psa 69:1-36</reference>. Upon Shoshannim--(See on <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Psa 45:1</reference>, title). Mingling the language of prayer and complaint, the sufferer, whose condition is here set forth, pleads for God's help as one suffering in His cause, implores the divine retribution on his malicious enemies, and, viewing his deliverance as sure, promises praise by himself, and others, to whom God will extend like blessings. This Psalm is referred to seven times in the New Testament as prophetical of Christ and the gospel times. Although the character in which the Psalmist appears to some in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.5">Psa 69:5</reference> is that of a sinner, yet his condition as a sufferer innocent of alleged crimes sustains the typical character of the composition, and it may be therefore regarded throughout, as the twenty-second, as typically expressive of the feelings of our Saviour in the flesh.</title> <div sID="gen9569" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6252"/>1-2. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6264"/><div sID="gen9584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6264"/>22-23. With unimportant verbal changes, this language is used by Paul to describe the rejection of the Jews who refused to receive the Saviour (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.9">Ro 11:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.10">10</reference>). The purport of the figures used is that blessings shall become curses, the "table" of joy (as one of food) a "snare," their<div eID="gen9584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">welfare--</hi>literally, "peaceful condition," or security, a "trap." Darkened eyes and failing strength complete the picture of the ruin falling on them under the invoked retribution. <div eID="gen9585" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 22-23. With unimportant verbal changes, this language is used by Paul to describe the rejection of the Jews who refused to receive the Saviour ( Ro 11:9 , 10 ). The purport of the figures used is that blessings shall become curses, the "table" of joy (as one of food) a "snare," their welfare-- literally, "peaceful condition," or security, a "trap." Darkened eyes and failing strength complete the picture of the ruin falling on them under the invoked retribution.

The call on the universe for praise is well sustained by the prediction of the perpetual and extended blessings which shall come upon the covenant-people of God. Though, as usual, the imagery is taken from terms used of Palestine, the whole tenor of the context indicates that the spiritual privileges and blessings of the Church are meant. <chapter eID="Ps.69"/>
